tr.td: Human scale
Corridor type, overall length, and pedestrian-scale spatial character
River-corridor/park transformation; more than 10 km long; pedestrian-scale landscape and public-realm elements distributed along the Manzanares corridor.
Urban arterial retrofit; approximately 2–3 km intervention corridor; widened sidewalks, tree alignments, and reallocated street space support a pedestrian-oriented boulevard character.
Major urban avenue; approximately 11 km long; selected remodeling sections increase pedestrian space through wider pavements, green infrastructure, and street furniture.
Large-scale linear urban corridor; 135 km planned length; organized through multiple destinations combining pedestrian and cycling routes with public-realm and recreational elements.
Human scale
Pedestrian-oriented space allocation and documented sidewalk width (where available)
A continuous linear corridor 120–200 m wide [43,44].
Reallocated road space through reduced parking and removal of a traffic lane; widened building-side sidewalks; 3 m central divider; cycle path on the west side [48].
Pavements widened to 7–7.5 m [47] in the documented redevelopment section; pedestrian promenade and cycling facilities improved [49].
Widened the sidewalks to approximately 12 m [41].
Human scale
Pedestrian-scale edges, street furniture, lighting, and landscape elements (where documented)

Landscape-based pedestrian public realm; which includes 12 pedestrian-bridges, 6 ha of public sports facilities, social, communal, and artistic amenities. Children’s areas and outdoor furniture [44,50].
Widened building-side sidewalks, five tree alignments, benches and outdoor terraces; pedestrian areas [48]. Supported by renovated LED lighting [51].
Remodeled and repaved pedestrian pavements with reallocated street space; new urban furniture and new lighting [47,52].

A landscaped public realm and various sports, cultural, and recreational facilities are integral to the project. The Design Code emphasizes lighting and pedestrian-focused urban design standards [5,41,53].
Walkability and active mobility
Continuity and accessibility of sidewalks and pedestrian routes
Riverside pedestrian network incorporating the 6 km Salón de Pinos walkway [43,44]. Universal-access compliance is not established by the cited description [54].
Building sidewalks widened; lowered pavement levels for people with reduced mobility documented within the wider Lisbon Central Axis scheme [48,51].
Pavements remodeled and repaved between Los Castillejos and Passeig de Sant Joan; continuous accessibility across the entire avenue is not established [52].
Pedestrian pathways incorporated across the project’s destinations [5].
Walkability and active mobility
Cycling route continuity and active-transport provision
Approximately 30 km of routes are shared by walkers and cyclists, connected with the Green Cycling Ring and other city cycling routes [54].
Cycle path incorporated into the widened western side divider [48] for calming and the prioritization of soft mobility [1,46].
Two-way cycle lane relocated along specified central-road and side-road sections; the documented intervention does not establish continuity along the entire avenue [52].
Provision for professional and amateur cycling, with dedicated cycling routes within destinations including the university loop and Sands Sports Park [5].
Walkability and active mobility
Crossing arrangements, traffic-space reallocation, and connections to destinations and public transport
Twelve new pedestrian bridges connect riverbank neighborhoods [50].
Parking reduction and reallocation of local access and public-transport connections are not specified in the cited project description.
Cycle-lane segregation at pedestrian crossings; coordination of bicycle and tram signals described as planned within the Glòries–Verdaguer tram-integration scheme [52].
Cycling bridge exceeding 900 m connects the Promenade and Wadi Hanifah; crossing spacing and public-transport access are not specified in the cited description [5,41].
Social interaction and placemaking
Seating, shaded rest areas, plazas, play spaces, recreational facilities, and public open spaces
Linear public park with 6 ha of public sports, social, communal, and artistic amenities; children’s areas, outdoor furniture, an urban beach, and landscaped public spaces [50].
Benches and outdoor terraces along widened sidewalks. Dedicated play spaces, plazas, and shaded rest areas are not specified in the reviewed project documentation [48].

The remodeled Los Castillejos section provides 17,290 m2 of additional pedestrian space and new street furniture including benches and lighting. The adjacent remodeled plaza Pablo Neruda provides an open gathering space [55].

Completed first-phase destinations like Wadi Hanifah and Promenade included green spaces, water features, walking trails, children’s playgrounds, cycling rest stops, retail, bicycle-service facilities, and art installations [5,41].
Contextual adaptation
Greening scale; planting and landscape strategy
The Salón de Pinos (Pine Lounge), a planting strategy of about 35,000 trees [43,44].
About 300 newly planted trees contribute to the boulevard’s public-realm setting [48].
About 8965 m2 of green space with parterres and 266 trees [55].
More than 13 km2 are planned to be dedicated to park space. Shade infrastructure, including tree canopies, shade structures and covered walkways [5,41].
Contextual adaptation
Climate context and environmental exposure
Mediterranean continental setting, with hot temperature; the river-corridor transformation responds primarily through ecological restoration, vegetation, and recovered public space [54].

Mediterranean climate, with exposure to summer heat, drought, and seasonal flooding; tree planting and widened pedestrian space are relevant within Lisbon’s wider green-infrastructure adaptation agenda [48].
Mediterranean climate, with summer heat, the documented section responds through increased pedestrian space, green infrastructure, and tree planting [55].
Hyper-arid desert context, with extreme summer heat, dust. The design prioritizes thermal comfort and water sensitivity, in addition to the use of shade infrastructure [5,41].
